content: Today marks the beginning of a new chapter in my life. After months of preparation, visa applications, and tearful goodbyes with family in Mumbai, I've finally arrived in Dublin to start my MSc in Computer Science at UCD. The flight was exhausting—nearly 14 hours with a layover in Dubai—but the excitement kept me going. Dublin greeted me with surprisingly pleasant weather, a gentle breeze rather than the legendary Irish rain I'd been warned about. My temporary accommodation is a small studio apartment in Smithfield, which I booked for the first month while I search for something more permanent and hopefully find roommates to share costs. The place is basic but clean, with a tiny kitchenette and a view of the city that's particularly beautiful as the sun sets. I spent most of the day unpacking and organizing my belongings, trying to make this foreign space feel somewhat like home. I hung up a small tapestry my mother insisted I bring—'to keep a piece of India with you,' she said—and arranged the collection of family photos on my desk. The jet lag is hitting hard now, but I forced myself to stay awake until a reasonable hour to adjust to the time zone. Tomorrow, I plan to explore the UCD campus and complete my registration in person. My mind is a whirlwind of emotions: excitement for the academic challenges ahead, anxiety about making friends and fitting in, and a persistent homesickness that I suspect will be my companion for at least the next few weeks. The pressure to succeed is immense—my parents have invested so much in this opportunity, and I'm determined not to let them down. I also can't help but think about the competitive job market that awaits after graduation. Will this degree truly open doors for me in Europe or back home? I've read so many success stories from Indian students abroad, but also tales of struggle and disappointment. Tonight, I'm choosing to focus on the positive. I'm here, in Ireland, about to study at one of the country's most prestigious universities. Whatever challenges come, I'll face them one day at a time.
project title: Arrival in Dublin: New Beginnings and Homesickness

content: Today was my first proper day in Dublin, and I decided to visit UCD campus before the orientation week officially begins. What a magnificent place! The campus is enormous compared to my undergraduate college in Mumbai, with modern buildings interspersed with green spaces and woodland walks. I spent nearly three hours just wandering around, locating the Computer Science building, the library, and other important facilities. The O'Brien Centre for Science is particularly impressive—a state-of-the-art complex where most of my classes will take place. I completed my registration process at the Student Desk, where the staff were incredibly helpful and patient with all my questions. They gave me my student card, which not only grants me access to university buildings but also serves as my library card. The internationalization office had a special desk for overseas students, and they provided me with a welcome pack containing essential information about healthcare, banking, transportation, and social activities. I met a few other international students during registration—a girl from China named Lin who's also doing Computer Science, and a Brazilian guy named Rafael who's studying Business Analytics. We exchanged phone numbers and agreed to attend the international student welcome reception together next week. It's reassuring to know I'm not the only one navigating this new experience. After leaving campus, I decided to be brave and explore Dublin city center. I took the bus (number 39A) from UCD to the city, which took about 30 minutes. The public transportation system seems efficient, though I'll need to get a Leap Card for regular travel. Walking around the city center was both exhilarating and overwhelming. The streets were bustling with people, street performers, and the distinctive sounds of Irish accents mixed with various languages from tourists and other international residents. I visited Trinity College briefly—UCD's historic rival, as I've been told—and walked along the River Liffey. The architecture is a fascinating blend of historic and modern, so different from Mumbai. My feet were aching by late afternoon, so I stopped at a small café called The Proper Order for coffee. The barista, noticing my confused examination of the menu, recommended an Americano and a scone. Both were delicious, though different from what I'm used to back home. The coffee culture here seems to be taken very seriously! I also stopped by a grocery store to stock up on essentials for my apartment. The prices gave me a bit of a shock—groceries are definitely more expensive here than in India, and I'll need to budget carefully. I bought some basic ingredients to cook simple meals for the next few days. As I returned to my apartment in the evening, I felt a wave of accomplishment mixed with exhaustion. This city is going to be my home for at least the next year, and there's so much to learn and adjust to. The academic challenges haven't even begun yet, and already I feel slightly overwhelmed by the cultural adaptation. But there's also an undeniable excitement about all the possibilities ahead. I've taken the first steps toward building a life here, however temporary it might be. Tomorrow, I plan to figure out banking and phone services, and perhaps explore the area around my apartment more thoroughly.
project title: First Look at UCD and Dublin City

content: Banking and bureaucracy dominated my day—necessary tasks that aren't particularly exciting but are crucial for settling in. I opened an account with Bank of Ireland, which has a branch on the UCD campus. The process was straightforward, though they needed quite a bit of documentation: my passport, student visa, UCD acceptance letter, and proof of address. Fortunately, I had brought multiple copies of everything from India, following advice from seniors who'd studied abroad. The bank staff assigned me a personal advisor who helped me understand the various account options and set up mobile banking. I opted for a student account that waives most fees and comes with a debit card, which should arrive within 5-7 working days. Until then, I'll have to rely on the cash I brought and my Indian credit card, which unfortunately charges foreign transaction fees. Next, I sorted out my phone situation by getting an Irish SIM card from Three, which offers a decent student plan with ample data. Having local phone service immediately made me feel more connected and secure. I also registered with the Irish Naturalisation and Immigration Service (INIS) as required for all non-EU students staying longer than 90 days. The queue was long, and the process took nearly two hours, but the officers were efficient and professional. My GNIB (Garda National Immigration Bureau) card will be ready for collection in two weeks. In the afternoon, I finally explored the neighborhood around my Smithfield apartment. This area has an interesting mix of historic buildings and modern developments. The famous Jameson Distillery is just around the corner, and there's a charming square with cafes and restaurants. I discovered a small Asian grocery store that stocks Indian spices and ingredients—a welcome find that will help me cook familiar foods when homesickness strikes. I treated myself to lunch at a place called Token, which combines a restaurant with retro arcade games. The atmosphere was lively, with people of all ages enjoying the games. I had a vegetarian burger that was surprisingly good, though not quite the taste of home I'm already missing. While eating, I overheard a group speaking in accented English that sounded Indian. I almost approached them but felt suddenly shy—something unusual for me. I realize I'm feeling vulnerable in this new environment, hesitant in ways I normally wouldn't be. Back at the apartment, I made a video call to my parents. Seeing their faces brought both comfort and a renewed wave of homesickness. They were eager to hear about everything, and I tried to sound positive and confident even while describing the challenges. My father, ever practical, asked about the university facilities and course structure, while my mother was more concerned about whether I'm eating properly and staying warm enough. I reassured them on all fronts, though I did mention the higher cost of living than we'd anticipated. They reminded me that my cousin Rajiv lives in Belfast, about two hours away by train, and suggested I reach out to him soon. It might be nice to connect with family, however distant. As I prepare for bed, I'm reflecting on these first few days of independence. Each small accomplishment—navigating public transport, opening a bank account, finding groceries—feels significant. I'm building the foundation for my life here, one administrative task at a time. Tomorrow brings the international student orientation, and I'm looking forward to meeting more people in similar situations.
project title: Settling In: Banking, Bureaucracy, and Local Exploration

content: The international student orientation today was a whirlwind of information, activities, and new faces. UCD has a remarkably diverse student body, with people from over 130 countries according to the welcome presentation. The main orientation session was held in the large O'Reilly Hall, which was packed with hundreds of international students. We received presentations from various university departments covering essential topics: academic expectations, health services, support resources, campus facilities, and safety information. A particularly useful session focused on understanding Irish academic culture, which apparently differs significantly from many other countries, including India. The emphasis here is on critical thinking and independent research rather than memorization and reproduction of material—something I'll need to adapt to quickly. After the general sessions, we broke into smaller groups based on our faculty. I joined the College of Science group, where we met some of the professors and administrative staff specific to our programs. Professor Brennan, who coordinates the MSc Computer Science program, gave us an overview of what to expect in the coming year. Her description of the Distributed Systems and Cloud Computing modules particularly excited me, as these are areas I'm keen to specialize in. During the lunch break, I reconnected with Lin and Rafael from yesterday and met several other Computer Science students: Akiko from Japan, Ibrahim from Nigeria, and Elena from Romania. We exchanged contact information and created a WhatsApp group named 'UCD CompSci International 2024.' It's reassuring to have this instant network of peers facing similar challenges. The afternoon featured a campus tour led by current students. Our guide, Patrick, is a final-year Computer Science undergraduate who offered valuable insights beyond the official information. He showed us the best quiet study spots in the library, which cafes offer student discounts, and even which professors are known for particularly challenging assessments. The tour ended at the Student Centre, where various clubs and societies had set up information booths. The diversity of options was impressive—everything from sports and academic societies to cultural and special interest groups. I signed up for the Indian Society, the Computing Society, and the Hiking Club, hoping these will provide both professional networking and social opportunities. In the evening, there was a welcome reception with refreshments, where I had longer conversations with some of the people I'd met earlier. Elena and I discovered we're both interested in machine learning applications, while Ibrahim has professional experience in software development that he's eager to build upon. Lin seemed quieter but opened up when discussing our shared anxiety about the workload ahead. As we talked about our backgrounds and aspirations, I felt a sense of connection forming. These might be the people who become my closest friends here, or at least my academic support network. Walking back to my apartment, I reflected on how quickly life can change. Just four days ago, I was saying goodbye to my family at Mumbai Airport, and now I'm forming new connections halfway across the world. The homesickness is still there, a dull ache beneath the excitement, but today helped me see the possibilities this year holds. The academic challenges will be significant—I'm under no illusions about that—but having met others on the same journey makes it seem more manageable. Tomorrow is the Computer Science program-specific orientation, which should provide more details about our modules, assessments, and faculty. I'm particularly keen to learn about research opportunities and industry connections, as gaining practical experience will be crucial for my post-graduation plans.
project title: UCD International Orientation: Information and Networking

content: Today's Computer Science program orientation gave me a much clearer picture of what lies ahead academically, and I'm both excited and intimidated by the journey. The day began with a welcome address from Professor Collins, the Head of School, who outlined the department's research strengths and industry connections. UCD's Computer Science department apparently has partnerships with major tech companies including Google, Microsoft, and several significant players in Ireland's thriving tech sector. This was encouraging to hear, as these connections could potentially lead to internship or employment opportunities. We then received detailed information about our specific MSc program. The Negotiated Learning pathway I've chosen offers considerable flexibility—after completing core modules in the first semester, I can specialize based on my interests and career goals. The program director emphasized that this approach requires self-direction and clear academic planning, which suits my learning style. The first semester modules were confirmed: Distributed Systems, Cloud Computing, Big Data, Machine Learning, and Text Analytics. Just reading the syllabi makes me realize how intensive this program will be. Each module involves lectures, labs, and substantial independent work, with assessments combining practical projects and theoretical examinations. Several professors introduced their modules briefly. Dr. Sharma, who teaches Machine Learning, was particularly engaging, describing fascinating applications of ML in various industries. His enthusiasm was contagious, and I'm now especially looking forward to that module, though it's reputed to be among the most challenging. We were also assigned academic advisors—mine is Dr. O'Connell, who specializes in distributed systems and cloud architecture. We'll meet next week to discuss my academic plan and any concerns I might have. After lunch, we had a practical session on using the university's online systems: Brightspace (the learning management system), the library databases, and various student services portals. While these systems seem well-designed, there's still a lot to navigate and remember. The afternoon included a panel discussion with current students and recent graduates of the program. Their insights were invaluable—they spoke candidly about workload management, recommended study strategies, and shared their experiences with group projects and assessments. One panelist, Mei, who graduated last year and now works at Accenture's Dublin office, emphasized the importance of building a portfolio of projects alongside coursework. Another, James, advised focusing on practical implementation skills rather than just theoretical knowledge, noting that recruiters particularly value problem-solving abilities. The most sobering part of the day was a session on academic integrity and plagiarism policies. The standards here seem much stricter than what I was accustomed to in India, with sophisticated plagiarism detection software and significant penalties for violations. I'll need to be extremely careful about proper citation and referencing in all my work. The day ended with a casual mixer where I had the chance to speak with some professors one-on-one. Dr. Sharma mentioned that he sometimes takes on research assistants from the master's program, which could be an excellent opportunity to gain research experience. I made sure to express my interest in Machine Learning applications for healthcare, which seemed to pique his curiosity. On my way home, I stopped by the university bookstore to purchase some recommended textbooks. The prices were higher than I expected—academic texts here cost significantly more than in India, even accounting for the exchange rate. I'll need to make greater use of the library and electronic resources to stay within my budget. This evening, I'm feeling a mix of enthusiasm and apprehension. The program promises to be intellectually stimulating but also incredibly demanding. The competitive atmosphere was palpable today, with many students clearly driven to excel. While I've always performed well academically, I wonder how I'll measure up in this international environment with different educational norms and expectations. Classes begin on Monday, and I'm determined to start strong, establish good study habits from the beginning, and make the most of every learning opportunity this program offers.
project title: Computer Science Orientation: Program Details and Expectations

content: With orientation week winding down, I decided to dedicate today to exploring Dublin more thoroughly and preparing for classes. The morning began with a trip to the campus bookstore to purchase the remaining course materials I need. I was pleasantly surprised to find some secondhand options that helped reduce the cost. A helpful staff member also pointed me toward online resources and open-access alternatives for some texts. Next, I visited the UCD library to familiarize myself with the layout and services. It's an impressive facility with multiple floors, specialized collections, and various study environments from silent individual carrels to collaborative spaces. I registered for a workshop on advanced database searching scheduled for next week, which should help with research for assignments. After leaving campus, I decided to explore Dublin's city center more systematically than my previous brief visit. I started at St. Stephen's Green, a beautiful park in the heart of the city, where locals were enjoying the surprisingly sunny weather. The landscaped gardens, duck ponds, and Victorian features created a peaceful oasis amid the urban bustle. From there, I walked down Grafton Street, Dublin's famous pedestrianized shopping area. Street performers created a lively atmosphere, and though most of the shops were beyond my student budget, it was entertaining to window-shop and observe the diverse crowd. I continued to Trinity College and took a proper look this time, admiring the historic architecture and cobblestone squares. While UCD's modern campus has its advantages, there's something special about Trinity's centuries of tradition visible in every stone. The highlight was Trinity's Old Library and the Book of Kells exhibition. I paid the student admission fee, which felt worthwhile for such a significant cultural experience. The Long Room library was breathtaking—tall shelves filled with ancient volumes, marble busts of great thinkers, and that distinctive smell of old books. The illuminated manuscripts were exquisite, remarkable testaments to human creativity and patience. After leaving Trinity, I wandered through Temple Bar, which was already filling with tourists despite the early hour. The colorful buildings and narrow streets have charm, though I've been warned by longer-term students that locals tend to avoid this area due to inflated prices and crowds. I found a small café called Queen of Tarts on Dame Street for a late lunch. The quiche and salad were delicious, though I'm still adjusting to Irish portion sizes, which tend to be larger than what I'm used to. While eating, I reviewed my course schedules and started organizing my study planner for the semester. The workload looks intense, with multiple assignments often due around the same time. Careful time management will be essential. In the afternoon, I took the DART train to Howth, a coastal village north of Dublin that several people had recommended. The journey offered beautiful views of Dublin Bay, and Howth itself was picturesque with its working harbor, fishing boats, and seafood restaurants. I walked part of the cliff path, which provided spectacular vistas of the coastline and Ireland's Eye, a small uninhabited island offshore. The sea air was invigorating, and the physical activity helped clear my mind after days of information overload. During my walk, I called my friend Varun back in Mumbai. Hearing his familiar voice and our shared references to places and people from home brought both comfort and a twinge of sadness. He's preparing for MBA entrance exams and seemed stressed but was genuinely interested in my experiences so far. I found myself downplaying some of my anxieties—a habit I should perhaps work on, as honest communication with friends will be important for maintaining those connections across distance. Returning to the city, I decided to be practical and visit a large Tesco supermarket to stock up on groceries more economically than the small shops near my apartment. I'm gradually figuring out local equivalents to familiar Indian ingredients and adapting my cooking accordingly. Tonight, I prepared a simple khichdi with modifications based on available ingredients—comfort food that reminded me of home while using local produce. As classes begin next week, I feel reasonably prepared but also aware of how much I still have to learn—not just academically but culturally. The Irish students I've met have been friendly but sometimes reference cultural touchstones or use slang that goes over my head. Integration will take time and effort beyond just academics. My goal for the weekend is to finalize my living situation (I have viewings for two potential shared accommodations tomorrow) and to review prerequisite material for my courses to ensure I start from a solid foundation.
project title: Exploring Dublin's Landmarks and Preparing for Classes

content: Housing search day—possibly one of the most stressful aspects of moving to a new country. Dublin's rental market is notoriously competitive and expensive, as I quickly discovered. I had arranged viewings for two shared accommodations today, both found through the UCD accommodation office's listings. The first viewing was in Ranelagh, supposedly a nice residential area about 25 minutes by bus from campus. I arrived early to explore the neighborhood, which indeed seemed pleasant with cafes, shops, and good transport links. However, the actual viewing was disappointing. The house was shared by five people, with the available room being the smallest—barely fitting a single bed and desk. For €850 per month (utilities not included), it seemed poor value, and the existing housemates, though polite, gave the impression they weren't particularly interested in adding an international student to their established group. The second viewing in Rathmines was more promising. The apartment is shared by three others—Aoife and Cian (both Irish) and Lisa (German). The room is reasonably sized with good natural light, and includes its own small bathroom. At €950 per month including utilities, it stretches my budget but seems to be the going rate for decent accommodation near the city center. The location is excellent, with frequent buses to UCD and easy access to shops and amenities. What really made a difference was the housemates' welcoming attitude. They invited me to sit down for tea after showing me the room and seemed genuinely interested in getting to know me. They explained their house routines, shared spaces, and expectations clearly. All three are young professionals rather than students—Aoife works in marketing, Cian in software development, and Lisa in pharmaceutical research. This could actually be an advantage, offering connections outside the academic bubble and a quieter study environment than typical student housing. I told them I needed to think it over but was definitely interested. As I left, Lisa mentioned they were hoping to decide by tomorrow evening, so I don't have much time to consider or look at other options. On my way back to my temporary accommodation, I called my parents to discuss the housing situation. They agreed that while the Rathmines option is expensive, having a comfortable and friendly living environment is worth the investment, especially given the academic pressures ahead. They also reminded me that we had budgeted for housing costs at approximately this level. With their support, I've decided to accept the Rathmines room and have emailed Aoife to confirm my interest. If all goes well, I can move in next weekend, which would give me stability before classes intensify. The rest of my day was spent preparing for the academic challenges ahead. I reviewed some fundamental concepts in programming and mathematics that will be relevant for my courses. I'm particularly concerned about the Machine Learning module, as it requires strong statistical knowledge. While I covered these topics in my undergraduate studies, I want to ensure my foundation is solid before building upon it. In the evening, I joined a video call with the Indian Society's committee members. They're organizing a welcome event for new Indian students next Friday, and I've volunteered to help with arrangements. The society seems active, with regular cultural celebrations, professional networking events, and social gatherings. It will be nice to connect with the Indian community here, though I'm equally committed to integrating with the broader international student body. Before bed, I exchanged messages with Akash, my closest friend from undergraduate days who's doing his master's at TU Delft in the Netherlands. We compared notes on our experiences so far—both the challenges and excitements of studying abroad. There's comfort in knowing someone who understands both where I'm coming from and what I'm going through now, even if we're in different countries. Tomorrow I plan to visit the campus once more to locate all my lecture venues before classes begin, and perhaps attend the Sunday service at the campus multi-faith center. Though I'm not particularly religious, the spiritual connection might provide some grounding as I navigate all these transitions.
project title: Securing Accommodation: The Dublin Housing Hunt

content: Sunday brought a welcome change of pace—less structured than the orientation days but still productive. I woke early and decided to attempt meditation, something I've practiced sporadically but want to make a regular habit here to manage stress. The quiet morning, with soft rain pattering against my window, created the perfect atmosphere for twenty minutes of mindfulness. After breakfast, I headed to campus with two objectives: locating my lecture venues and visiting the sports facilities I hadn't yet explored. The Sunday campus had a different energy—quieter but not deserted, with some students already in the library and others enjoying the common spaces. I methodically found each building and room on my timetable, taking photos of locations and noting the most efficient routes between classes. This should help reduce stress during the first week when everything else will be new and demanding. The UCD Sport and Fitness Center impressed me with its comprehensive facilities: a 50-meter pool, gym, sports halls, and various courts and pitches. The membership fee for students is reasonable, and I decided to join, considering physical activity crucial for maintaining mental health during intensive study periods. I signed up for a Tuesday evening beginner's swimming improvement class—swimming is a skill I've always wanted to develop better. As planned, I attended the multi-faith center's Sunday gathering. It wasn't a traditional religious service but rather an inclusive spiritual reflection led by the university chaplain. The theme was 'Beginning Journeys,' appropriately enough, with readings from various faith traditions about setting out into the unknown. The diverse attendees—people of different nationalities, faiths, and ages—created a warm, accepting atmosphere. During the social time afterward, I met Olamide from Nigeria and Catalina from Chile, both postgraduate students in different disciplines. Catalina has been in Dublin for a year already and offered practical advice about everything from weather-appropriate clothing to finding authentic international groceries. In the afternoon, I received good news—Aoife confirmed that I can move into the Rathmines apartment next Saturday. The relief of having permanent housing arranged lifted a significant weight from my shoulders. I immediately began planning the move and budgeting for initial expenses like the security deposit and first month's rent. With housing secured, I turned my attention to financial planning more broadly. I created a detailed spreadsheet tracking my expenses so far and projecting costs for the academic year. Between tuition, rent, food, transport, books, and modest social activities, it's going to be tight but manageable if I'm careful. I might need to look for part-time work after I settle into the academic routine, though I'm hesitant to commit to anything that might compromise my studies. Early evening brought a video call with my parents and younger sister. They were relieved about my housing situation and excited to see glimpses of my temporary apartment and the photos I'd taken around Dublin. My sister, who's preparing for her engineering entrance exams, seemed particularly interested in the university facilities. Perhaps she'll consider international study in a few years too. I spent the remainder of the evening reviewing material for tomorrow's first classes: Distributed Systems and Machine Learning. The syllabi indicate challenging content from the very beginning, with no gentle introduction period. Distributed Systems will begin with fundamental concepts of concurrency and communication, while Machine Learning jumps straight into supervised learning algorithms. I feel reasonably prepared but also aware that the teaching style and expectations may differ significantly from what I'm used to. As I prepare for bed, a mixture of excitement and nervousness dominates my thoughts. Tomorrow represents the true beginning of this academic journey—the real reason I've traveled thousands of miles from home. I'm setting my alarm early to ensure a calm morning routine before facing whatever challenges the day brings.
project title: Final Preparations: Campus, Housing, and Finances

content: First day of classes—a milestone that's both exhilarating and intimidating. I woke before my alarm, a sign of either anxiety or eagerness, perhaps both. After a quick breakfast and last review of my schedule, I headed to campus for my 9 AM Distributed Systems lecture. The Computer Science building was buzzing with activity, students huddled in groups or hurrying to classes. Finding my lecture hall was straightforward thanks to yesterday's reconnaissance. The classroom filled quickly with about sixty students, predominantly male but with better gender diversity than my undergraduate computer science classes in India. Professor O'Malley began precisely on time with a no-nonsense introduction to the course structure, assessment methods, and his expectations. His teaching style is direct and fast-paced, with an assumption that students will speak up if they don't understand something—quite different from the more hierarchical teacher-student dynamic I'm accustomed to. The lecture content moved quickly through foundational concepts of distributed systems, touching on challenges like concurrency, consistency, and fault tolerance. The technical content wasn't entirely new to me, but the perspective and depth were more advanced than my previous exposure. I found myself taking rapid notes, trying to capture both the factual information and the professor's insights from industry experience. After a short break, my Machine Learning class began at 11 AM. Dr. Sharma, whose enthusiasm had impressed me during orientation, maintained that energy in the lecture theater. The class is larger—about a hundred students from various master's programs and disciplines. Dr. Sharma began with a provocative question about the ethical implications of ML in decision-making systems, immediately engaging the class in discussion. This interactive approach continued throughout the session, with students encouraged to contribute perspectives and questions. The technical content was challenging, with Dr. Sharma assuming strong mathematical foundations, particularly in linear algebra and probability theory. Some concepts were familiar from my undergraduate studies, but the mathematical rigor was definitely elevated. I noticed several students looking confused during explanations of feature spaces and hyperplane geometry, which made me grateful for my solid mathematics background. Between classes, I met up with Lin and Elena from orientation week. We compared initial impressions and agreed to form a study group for Machine Learning, which seems likely to be particularly demanding. During lunch at the campus restaurant, we were joined by Alejandro from Mexico and Siobhan, an Irish student who completed her undergraduate degree at UCD. Siobhan offered valuable insights about professors' assessment styles and recommended resources beyond the official reading lists. The afternoon brought my first lab session for Distributed Systems. The computer labs at UCD are impressive—high-specification machines and plenty of technical support staff. We worked through practical exercises implementing simple distributed algorithms in Java. I paired with Ibrahim, whom I'd met during orientation. He has professional experience with distributed systems from his work in Nigeria, which complemented my more theoretical knowledge. We worked well together, finishing the assigned tasks with time to spare. After classes, I attended the Computing Society's first meeting of the semester. About thirty students gathered to hear the committee's plans for the year, which include industry talks, hackathons, coding competitions, and social events. I signed up for their mailing list and introduced myself to a few members. David, the society president, mentioned they're looking for postgraduate representatives on the committee—something to consider once I've settled into the academic routine. By evening, I was mentally exhausted but satisfied with the day's experiences. Returning to my apartment, I organized my notes and began the recommended readings for next week's classes. The reading load is substantial, with multiple papers assigned for each module. I'll need to develop efficient reading strategies to manage the volume without sacrificing comprehension. As I reflect on this first day, I'm struck by the different educational culture here. There's an expectation of student initiative, critical engagement with material, and contribution to discussions that goes beyond what was typically expected in my undergraduate environment. Adapting to this culture while managing the technical demands of the coursework will be challenging but potentially very rewarding. Tomorrow brings two more new modules—Cloud Computing and Text Analytics—and I'm curious to see how they compare to today's experiences. Despite the academic intensity, I'm genuinely excited about the content and the learning opportunities ahead.
project title: First Day of Lectures: Diving into Coursework

content: Second day of classes brought two new modules into focus: Cloud Computing and Text Analytics. The contrast between these classes highlighted the breadth of my chosen program and the diverse teaching approaches within the department. Cloud Computing with Dr. Jensen began at 10 AM in one of the newer lecture theaters. The class size is moderate—about forty students—and seems to attract those with specific interests in infrastructure and systems architecture. Dr. Jensen's approach is highly practical, drawing on her extensive industry experience with major cloud providers before joining academia. She began by outlining the evolution of cloud technologies and current industry trends before delving into service models (IaaS, PaaS, SaaS) and deployment approaches. What particularly impressed me was how she connected theoretical concepts to real-world implementations, referencing specific services from AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud. This applied perspective will be valuable for future employment. The assessment structure for this module is project-heavy, with 70% of our grade coming from a semester-long practical implementation involving cloud architecture design, deployment, and optimization. We'll be working in teams of three, with groups to be formed next week. This practical emphasis aligns well with my learning preferences, though I'm slightly apprehensive about the team dynamics with people I don't yet know well. After lunch, Text Analytics with Professor Garcia presented a complete shift in both content and teaching style. This module sits at the intersection of computational linguistics, information retrieval, and machine learning—an area relatively new to me. Professor Garcia's teaching style is more traditional and structured than the interactive approaches of yesterday's professors. He methodically outlined the field's key concepts, historical development, and current applications, occasionally illustrating points with examples from his research in sentiment analysis of social media content. The mathematical foundations of text processing techniques were covered thoroughly, with particular attention to vector space models and similarity metrics. While some concepts connected with the machine learning material from yesterday, the linguistic aspects introduced entirely new territory for me. The module will involve regular programming assignments in Python, beginning next week with basic text preprocessing techniques. I'm comfortable with Python but less familiar with some of the specialized libraries mentioned, like NLTK and spaCy, so I've added tutorials on these to my study plan. My final commitment today was the Big Data introductory lecture with Dr. O'Donnell. This late afternoon session (4-6 PM) proved challenging after a full day of concentration, but the content was engaging enough to maintain my attention. Dr. O'Donnell's enthusiasm for massive data processing techniques was evident as she described applications ranging from genomics to smart city infrastructure. The technical focus on distributed processing frameworks like Hadoop and Spark will complement the Distributed Systems module nicely. Between classes, I managed to connect with more classmates. Rohan, another Indian student who completed his undergraduate degree at VIT Vellore, shared his first impressions and concerns similar to mine about adapting to the different academic expectations. We agreed to meet for coffee later this week to discuss our adjustment strategies. I also formally introduced myself to Dr. O'Connell, my assigned academic advisor, and scheduled our first meeting for Friday morning. During a break, I called the Rathmines apartment to confirm details for Saturday's move. Aoife answered and reassured me that everything is arranged—I'll get keys and complete paperwork when I arrive. She mentioned that they're planning a small welcome dinner that evening, which was an unexpectedly kind gesture that made me feel more confident about my housing choice. The day ended with my first proper exploration of the UCD library's electronic resources. The database access here is impressive, with subscriptions to all major computer science journals and conference proceedings. I spent an hour learning to navigate the search interfaces and reference management tools, which should streamline my research process for assignments. Returning to my temporary accommodation, exhaustion hit hard. Five hours of lectures plus independent study time has made these first days mentally demanding. Distributed Systems today explored failure detection mechanisms in distributed environments—a topic combining theoretical elegance with substantial practical implications. Professor O'Malley described various algorithms for detecting node failures and managing system reconfiguration, evaluating their tradeoffs in accuracy, speed, and communication overhead. The mathematics underlying probabilistic failure detection was particularly interesting, demonstrating how theoretical computer science concepts directly inform practical system design. The lecture concluded with a case study of Amazon's Dynamo database, illustrating how these principles are implemented in production systems supporting global-scale applications. The Machine Learning lecture continued our exploration of classification algorithms, focusing today on decision trees and ensemble methods. Dr. Sharma demonstrated how combining multiple "weak" learners can create powerful classification systems, explaining the mathematical foundations of random forests and gradient boosting approaches. The concept of bias-variance tradeoff was central to today's discussion, providing a theoretical framework for understanding algorithm selection and parameter tuning. I'm finding that my background in statistical theory is proving valuable for following these mathematically rigorous explanations. After the lecture, Dr. Sharma announced a special guest lecture next week by a researcher from the SFI Centre for Machine Learning. This collaborative learning approach is proving valuable for reinforcing individual understanding while gaining exposure to different perspectives. Dr. Sharma specifically commended my clear mathematical derivations and thoughtful discussion of real-world implications. This validation of my academic capabilities in this challenging course has significantly boosted my confidence. It confirms that despite differences in educational background and culture, I can excel in this international academic environment. The presentation focused on scalable system design principles, with case studies from Google's infrastructure. The content complemented our Distributed Systems and Cloud Computing coursework perfectly, providing industry context for academic concepts. During the networking session afterward, I introduced myself to the speaker and asked about internship opportunities. He recommended applying for Google's summer internship program, which opens applications in October, and suggested specific project areas that align with my interests in distributed systems and cloud infrastructure. This kind of direct industry connection represents exactly the professional networking opportunity I hoped for when choosing to study internationally.
